claim: HAND persists in treated patients as a result of chronic inflammation and low-level expression of viral proteins.
source: HAND persists in treated patients as a result of chronic inflammation and low-level expression of viral proteins, though the mechanisms involved in synaptic damage are unclear.
evidence: This is a statement about the persistence of HAND in treated patients, presented as established knowledge in the field.

claim: CXCL12 recoups both cognitive performance and synaptodendritic health in a rodent model of HAND.
source: Here, we report that the chemokine CXCL12 recoups both cognitive performance and synaptodendritic health in a rodent model of HAND, which recapitulates the neuroinflammatory state of virally controlled individuals and the associated structural/functional deficiencies.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: CXCL12 preferentially regulates plastic thin spines on layer II/III pyramidal neurons of the medial prefrontal cortex.
source: CXCL12 preferentially regulates plastic thin spines on layer II/III pyramidal neurons of the medial prefrontal cortex via CXCR4-dependent stimulation of the Rac1/PAK actin polymerization pathway, leading to increased spine density and improved flexible behavior.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data on spine morphology and density measurements.

claim: CXCL12 acts via CXCR4-dependent stimulation of the Rac1/PAK actin polymerization pathway.
source: CXCL12 preferentially regulates plastic thin spines on layer II/III pyramidal neurons of the medial prefrontal cortex via CXCR4-dependent stimulation of the Rac1/PAK actin polymerization pathway, leading to increased spine density and improved flexible behavior.
evidence: This is supported by mechanistic studies showing CXCR4 and Rac1/PAK pathway involvement.

claim: CXCL12 signaling leads to increased spine density and improved flexible behavior.
source: CXCL12 preferentially regulates plastic thin spines on layer II/III pyramidal neurons of the medial prefrontal cortex via CXCR4-dependent stimulation of the Rac1/PAK actin polymerization pathway, leading to increased spine density and improved flexible behavior.
evidence: This is supported by both structural (spine density) and behavioral (cognitive flexibility) data.

claim: HAND may be reversible and upturned by targeting Rac1-dependent processes in cortical neurons.
source: Our studies unveil a critical role of CXCL12/CXCR4 signaling in spine dynamics and cognitive flexibility, suggesting that HAND - or other diseases driven by spine loss - may be reversible and upturned by targeting Rac1-dependent processes in cortical neurons.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the experimental findings showing recovery with CXCL12 treatment.

claim: Approximately 30–50% of HIV+ infected patients will develop some form of neurocognitive dysfunction.
source: While the introduction of combination antiretroviral therapy (ART) has significantly reduced the severity of neurological impairments in HIV+ individuals, approximately 30–50% of infected patients will develop some form of neurocognitive dysfunction (Saylor et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Saylor et al., 2016.

claim: Neurocognitive impairments continue to be important determinants of quality of life and disease progression in HIV+ patients.
source: Additionally, these impairments continue to be important determinants of quality of life, as well as disease progression (Simioni et al., 2010; Tozzi et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Simioni et al., 2010 and Tozzi et al., 2007.

claim: The neuropathology of HAND has shifted dramatically since the implementation of ART.
source: The neuropathology of HAND is complex and has shifted dramatically since the implementation of ART (McArthur et al., 2010); however, the presence of chronic, low-level inflammation and viral neurotoxins disrupt neuroprotective and bioenergetic mechanisms that converge on aberrant synaptodendritic pruning and functional alterations in neurons (González-Scarano and Martín-García, 2005; Raybuck et al., 2017; Sanchez et al., 2016; Sanna et al., 2017; Saylor et al., 2016; Stern et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to McArthur et al., 2010.

claim: Chronic, low-level inflammation and viral neurotoxins disrupt neuroprotective and bioenergetic mechanisms that converge on aberrant synaptodendritic pruning and functional alterations in neurons.
source: The neuropathology of HAND is complex and has shifted dramatically since the implementation of ART (McArthur et al., 2010); however, the presence of chronic, low-level inflammation and viral neurotoxins disrupt neuroprotective and bioenergetic mechanisms that converge on aberrant synaptodendritic pruning and functional alterations in neurons (González-Scarano and Martín-García, 2005; Raybuck et al., 2017; Sanchez et al., 2016; Sanna et al., 2017; Saylor et al., 2016; Stern et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations including González-Scarano and Martín-García, 2005; Raybuck et al., 2017; Sanchez et al., 2016; Sanna et al., 2017; Saylor et al., 2016; Stern et al., 2018.

claim: A reduction in the number of dendritic spines in the frontal cortex of HIV+ patients is significantly correlated with neurocognitive impairment.
source: A reduction in the number of dendritic spines, the main sites of excitatory neurotransmission, in the frontal cortex of HIV+ patients is significantly correlated with neurocognitive impairment (HNRC Group et al., 1999; Masliah et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citations to HNRC Group et al., 1999 and Masliah et al., 1997.

claim: The reduction in dendritic spines in HIV+ patients has been recapitulated in the HIV-1 transgenic (HIV-Tg) rat model.
source: This finding has been recapitulated in animal models of HAND, including the non-infectious HIV-1 transgenic (HIV-Tg) rat (Festa et al., 2015; Reid et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Festa et al., 2015 and Reid et al., 2001.

claim: HIV-Tg rats recapitulate key neurochemical, genetic, and behavioral features of the human HAND pathology as seen in treated patients.
source: HIV-Tg rats are being increasingly used in HAND research, as they recapitulate key neurochemical, genetic, and behavioral features of the human pathology as seen in treated patients, such as undetectable viral replication, reduction of post-synaptic markers, neuroinflammation, changes in gene expression, and behavioral deficits (Festa et al., 2015; Homji et al., 2012; June et al., 2009; McLaurin et al., 2017; Reid et al., 2001; Repunte-Canonigo et al., 2014; Royal et al., 2012; Vigorito et al., 2015; Wayman et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations including Festa et al., 2015; Homji et al., 2012; June et al., 2009; McLaurin et al., 2017; Reid et al., 2001; Repunte-Canonigo et al., 2014; Royal et al., 2012; Vigorito et al., 2015; Wayman et al., 2016.

claim: Viral proteins are expressed at low levels in the brain of HIV-Tg rats, including in the prefrontal cortex.
source: In these animals, as in patients, viral proteins are expressed at low levels in the brain - including in the prefrontal cortex, an area involved in higher cognitive functions and neuroHIV (Ann et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Ann et al., 2016.

claim: CXCL12 and its main signaling receptor CXCR4 regulate several critical steps of CNS development, including neuronal survival and neuronal-glial communication.
source: The chemokine CXCL12 and its main signaling receptor CXCR4 regulate several critical steps of CNS development, including neuronal survival and neuronal-glial communication (Bhattacharyya et al., 2008; Guyon and Nahon, 2007; Khan et al., 2004; Nicolai et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Bhattacharyya et al., 2008; Guyon and Nahon, 2007; Khan et al., 2004; Nicolai et al., 2010.

claim: CXCL12 could modulate spine morphology in mature neurons.
source: Our previous findings in differentiated central neurons suggested that the chemokine could also modulate spine morphology, an important factor for input-specific alterations in synaptic strength (Yuste, 2011), particularly in the mature brain.
evidence: This is based on previous findings and supported by a citation to Yuste, 2011.

claim: Dendritic protrusions are often grouped into four major classes: mushroom, thin, and stubby spines and filopodia.
source: Dendritic protrusions are often grouped into four major classes: mushroom, thin, and stubby spines and filopodia (Peters and Kaiserman-Abramof, 1970).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation to Peters and Kaiserman-Abramof, 1970.

claim: Mushroom and thin spines are classically considered mature structures, while stubby spines and filopodia are thought of as immature or spine precursors.
source: Mushroom and thin spines are classically considered mature structures, while stubby spines and filopodia are thought of as immature or spine precursors, respectively (Bourne and Harris, 2007).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation to Bourne and Harris, 2007.

claim: ICV administration of CXCL12 completely rescues dendritic spine loss in the HIV-Tg rat.
source: Here, we report that intracebroventricular (ICV) administration of CXCL12 completely rescues dendritic spine loss and cognitive dysfunction in the HIV-Tg rat.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data.

claim: ICV administration of CXCL12 completely rescues cognitive dysfunction in the HIV-Tg rat.
source: Here, we report that intracebroventricular (ICV) administration of CXCL12 completely rescues dendritic spine loss and cognitive dysfunction in the HIV-Tg rat.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data.

claim: CXCL12 specifically increased the number of thin spines in layer II/III pyramidal neurons of the medial prefrontal cortex.
source: The chemokine specifically increased the number of thin spines, which are associated with learning and plasticity, in layer II/III pyramidal neurons of the medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data on spine morphology.

claim: Thin spines are associated with learning and plasticity.
source: The chemokine specifically increased the number of thin spines, which are associated with learning and plasticity, in layer II/III pyramidal neurons of the medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC).
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field of neuroscience.

claim: Upregulation of spine density by CXCL12 correlates with an improvement in cognitive flexibility.
source: In the same animals, upregulation of spine density by CXCL12 correlates with an improvement in cognitive flexibility, a task mediated by the mPFC.
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis between spine density and behavioral performance.

claim: Cognitive flexibility is a task mediated by the mPFC.
source: In the same animals, upregulation of spine density by CXCL12 correlates with an improvement in cognitive flexibility, a task mediated by the mPFC.
evidence: This is established knowledge in neuroscience.

claim: The Rac1/PAK pathway plays an essential role in mediating the effects of CXCL12 on dendritic spines and cognition.
source: Our mechanistic studies demonstrate the essential role of the Rac1/PAK pathway in mediating the effects of CXCL12 on dendritic spines and cognition.
evidence: This is supported by mechanistic studies using Rac1 inhibitors and knockdown experiments.

claim: HIV-Tg rats performed worse on the position discrimination task compared to age- and sex-matched WT animals.
source: In the first two phases of the task (position discrimination and position reversal), there was a slight but significant difference between WT and Tg rats for position discrimination (30.17 ± 2.212 TTC for WT compared to 52.50 ± 11.90 TTC for Tg; Figure 1A)
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: No significant difference was observed between WT and HIV-Tg rats on position reversal.
source: and none observed for position reversal (81.17 ± 18.11 TTC for WT compared to 64.50 ± 4.19 TTC for Tg; Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: HIV-Tg rats performed significantly worse than control animals in the shift to cue phase.
source: In the shift to cue phase, however, Tg rats performed significantly worse than control animals (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Only four out of six HIV-Tg animals reached criterion by day 10 of the set-shifting phase.
source: Only four out of six Tg animals reached criterion by day 10 of the set-shifting phase and those who did complete the task took significantly longer to reach criterion (949.5 ± 146.3 TTC compared to 350.8 ± 84 TTC for WT).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data.

claim: HIV-Tg animals that completed the set-shifting task took significantly longer to reach criterion compared to WT animals.
source: Only four out of six Tg animals reached criterion by day 10 of the set-shifting phase and those who did complete the task took significantly longer to reach criterion (949.5 ± 146.3 TTC compared to 350.8 ± 84 TTC for WT).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data.

claim: A different curve was best fit for each group (WT vs HIV-Tg) in the cumulative proportion of animals reaching criterion over sessions.
source: Additionally, a linear regression analysis on the cumulative proportion of animals reaching criterion over sessions revealed that a different curve was best fit for each group (F(1,11)=15.94, p=0.0021) further illustrating the gap between the groups in the number of sessions needed to reach criterion (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis and shown in Figure 1D.

claim: HIV-Tg rats had significantly reduced dendritic spine density in layer II/III pyramidal neurons in the mPFC compared to control animals.
source: Compared with control animals, Tg rats had significantly reduced dendritic spine density, as we previously observed in older animals (Festa et al., 2015) (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by spine density measurements shown in Figure 2A and cited previous work.

claim: The density of thin spines was reduced in HIV-Tg rats compared to WT controls.
source: In addition to spine density, subtle spine morphological changes were also present, whereby the density of thin (Figure 2B) and mushroom spines was reduced (Figure 2C), while stubby spines were upregulated (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by spine morphology analysis shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The density of mushroom spines was reduced in HIV-Tg rats compared to WT controls.
source: In addition to spine density, subtle spine morphological changes were also present, whereby the density of thin (Figure 2B) and mushroom spines was reduced (Figure 2C), while stubby spines were upregulated (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by spine morphology analysis shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Stubby spine density was upregulated in HIV-Tg rats compared to WT controls.
source: In addition to spine density, subtle spine morphological changes were also present, whereby the density of thin (Figure 2B) and mushroom spines was reduced (Figure 2C), while stubby spines were upregulated (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by spine morphology analysis shown in Figure 2D.

claim: There is a shift in spine morphology from mature (mushroom and thin) to immature (stubby) in HIV-Tg rats.
source: This demonstrates a shift in spine morphology from mature (mushroom and thin) to immature (stubby), which is expected to alter cognition.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the spine morphology data.

claim: Spine density in the mPFC was negatively correlated with performance on the shift to cue phase.
source: Indeed, spine density in the mPFC was negatively correlated with performance to the shift to cue phase (Pearson's r = −0.7368, p=0.0151, α = 0.05; Figure 2E)
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The relationship between spine density and shift to cue performance became stronger when only thin spine density was considered.
source: and this relationship became stronger when only thin spine density was considered (Pearson's r = −0.7920, p=0.0063, α = 0.05; Figure 2F).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Spine density in the mPFC was not correlated with performance on position discrimination.
source: On the contrary, spine density in the mPFC was not correlated with performance on position discrimination (Pearson's r = −0.4548, p=0.1374, α = 0.05)
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Spine density in the mPFC was not correlated with performance on position reversal.
source: or position reversal (Pearson's r = 0.4862, p=0.1090, α = 0.05; Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Both vehicle- and CXCL12-treated groups of HIV-Tg rats performed similarly across the first two phases (position discrimination and position reversal) of the behavioral task.
source: Both groups performed similarly across the first two phases (position discrimination and position reversal) of the behavioral task, with animals reaching criterion in approximately one day (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: CXCL12-treated HIV-Tg rats took significantly fewer trials to reach criterion than vehicle-treated counterparts in the shift to cue task.
source: In the shift to cue task, CXCL12-treated rats took significantly fewer trials to reach criterion than vehicle-treated counterparts (for animals who reached criterion: 701.3 ± 97.26 TTC for CXCL12 compared to 1191 ± 114.5 TTC for vehicle).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data.

claim: A greater number of CXCL12-treated HIV-Tg rats completed the shift to cue task compared to vehicle-treated animals.
source: Additionally, a greater number of rats given CXCL12 (n = 7 out of 10) completed the task compared to vehicle-treated animals (n = 2 out of 9; p=0.03; Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: CXCL12-treated HIV-Tg rats completed the shift to cue task at a significantly faster rate than vehicle-treated rats.
source: A linear regression analysis on the cumulative proportion of animals reaching criterion over the ten sessions demonstrated that the CXCL12-treated rats completed the task at a significantly faster rate, F(1,16)=44.3781, p<0.001 (Figure 3B)
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis and shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Long term exposure to CXCL12 does not result in any deleterious effects on cognition in WT rats as measured by the attentional set-shifting task.
source: Parallel studies in male WT rats (Figure 3—figure supplement 3) showed that vehicle- and CXCL12-treated WT rodents performed at a similar level across all three phases of the task, indicating that long term exposure to CXCL12 does not result in any deleterious effects on cognition as measured by the attentional set-shifting task.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: Once-a-day infusion with CXCL12 significantly upregulated overall dendritic spine density in HIV-Tg rats.
source: Once-a-day infusion with CXCL12 significantly upregulated overall dendritic spine density (Figure 3C,D)
evidence: This is supported by spine density measurements shown in Figure 3C and 3D.

claim: CXCL12 treatment increased the number of thin spines in HIV-Tg rats.
source: as well as the number of thin spines (Figure 3E)
evidence: This is supported by spine morphology analysis shown in Figure 3E.

claim: CXCL12 treatment decreased stubby spine density in HIV-Tg rats.
source: while also decreasing stubby spine density (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is supported by spine morphology analysis shown in Figure 3F.

claim: There were no observed changes in mushroom spines or filopodia following CXCL12 treatment in HIV-Tg rats.
source: There were no observed changes in mushroom spines or filopodia.
evidence: This is a negative finding from the spine morphology analysis.

claim: Overall spine density in CXCL12-treated HIV-Tg rats was not significantly different from WT rats treated with vehicle.
source: Strikingly, overall spine density in CXCL12-treated Tg rats was not significantly different from WT rats treated with vehicle, consistent with the complete recovery of behavior we observed in these rodents (Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is supported by spine density comparison shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4.

claim: Overall spine density in the mPFC was negatively correlated with trials to criterion in the shift to cue phase in CXCL12-treated HIV-Tg rats.
source: Overall spine density in the mPFC was negatively correlated with trials to criterion in the shift to cue phase (Pearson's r = −0.7676, p=0.0157, α = 0.05; Figure 3G)
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 3G.

claim: Thin spine density demonstrated an even stronger relationship with performance on the shift to cue phase than overall spine density.
source: while thin spine density demonstrated an even stronger relationship with performance (Pearson's r = −0.8493, p=0.0038, α = 0.05; Figure 3H).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 3H.

claim: CXCL12 can activate the small Rho GTPase Rac1 in non-neuronal cells.
source: There is substantial evidence in non-neuronal cells that CXCL12 can activate the small Rho GTPase, Ras-related C3 botulinum toxin substrate 1 (Rac1) that acts as a critical regulator of actin polymerization and stabilization.
evidence: This is established knowledge from studies in non-neuronal cells.

claim: Rac1 acts as a critical regulator of actin polymerization and stabilization.
source: There is substantial evidence in non-neuronal cells that CXCL12 can activate the small Rho GTPase, Ras-related C3 botulinum toxin substrate 1 (Rac1) that acts as a critical regulator of actin polymerization and stabilization.
evidence: This is established knowledge in cell biology.

claim: When Rac1 is in its active form, it is bound to GTP.
source: When Rac1 is in its active form, it is bound to GTP, which allows it to physically interact with the serine/threonine kinase PAK1.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Rac1 function.

claim: Active Rac1 (bound to GTP) physically interacts with the serine/threonine kinase PAK1.
source: When Rac1 is in its active form, it is bound to GTP, which allows it to physically interact with the serine/threonine kinase PAK1.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Rac1-PAK1 interaction.

claim: CXCL12 significantly upregulates levels of Rac1-GTP at both 5 and 15 min in cultured cortical neurons.
source: In line with previous reports in non-neuronal cells, CXCL12 significantly upregulates levels of Rac1-GTP at both 5 and 15 min with a return to basal levels by 30 min (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by Rac1 activity assay data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: CXCL12-induced Rac1-GTP levels return to basal levels by 30 min in cultured cortical neurons.
source: In line with previous reports in non-neuronal cells, CXCL12 significantly upregulates levels of Rac1-GTP at both 5 and 15 min with a return to basal levels by 30 min (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by Rac1 activity assay data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: CXCL12 does not alter total levels of Rac1 in cultured cortical neurons.
source: Furthermore, there were no alterations in the total levels of Rac1, demonstrating that CXCL12 is altering the amount bound to GTP.
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data for total Rac1.

claim: Pretreatment with the CXCR4 antagonist AMD3100 attenuated CXCL12-induced activation of Rac1 in cortical neurons.
source: Pretreatment with either the specific CXCR4 inhibitor (AMD3100; 100 ng/mL, 20 min) or PTX (100 ng/mL, 18 hr) completely blocks the ability of CXCL12 to activate Rac1 in cortical neurons (Figure 4B and C).
evidence: This is supported by Rac1 activity assay data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Pretreatment with pertussis toxin (PTX) completely blocked CXCL12-induced activation of Rac1 in cortical neurons.
source: Pretreatment with either the specific CXCR4 inhibitor (AMD3100; 100 ng/mL, 20 min) or PTX (100 ng/mL, 18 hr) completely blocks the ability of CXCL12 to activate Rac1 in cortical neurons (Figure 4B and C).
evidence: This is supported by Rac1 activity assay data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: CXCR4 and its coupling to pertussis-toxin sensitive Gαi proteins is essential for the ability of CXCL12 to upregulate dendritic spine density.
source: CXCR4 and its coupling to pertussis-toxin (PTX) sensitive Gαi proteins is essential for the ability of CXCL12 to upregulate dendritic spine density (Pitcher et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Pitcher et al., 2014.

claim: CXCL12 treatment resulted in a time-dependent increase in phosphorylation of PAK1, LIMK1, and cofilin in cortical neurons.
source: In CXCL12-treated neurons, we observed a time-dependent increase in phosphorylation in PAK1 (Thr423), LIMK1 (Tyr507/508), and cofilin (Ser3) (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Inhibition of CXCR4 completely blocked CXCL12-induced phosphorylation of PAK1, LIMK1, and cofilin.
source: In line with our observations regarding Rac1 activation, inhibition of CXCR4 and Gαi signaling completely blocked CXCL12-induced phosphorylation of PAK1, LIMK1, and cofilin (Figure 5B and C).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Inhibition of Gαi signaling completely blocked CXCL12-induced phosphorylation of PAK1, LIMK1, and cofilin.
source: In line with our observations regarding Rac1 activation, inhibition of CXCR4 and Gαi signaling completely blocked CXCL12-induced phosphorylation of PAK1, LIMK1, and cofilin (Figure 5B and C).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: CXCL12 increased phosphorylation of SSH1 after one hour in cortical neurons.
source: CXCL12 increased phosphorylation of SSH1 after one hour, demonstrating that not only does CXCL12 regulate the phosphorylation status of LIMK1 and cofilin through activation of Rac1 and PAK1, but also through inactivation of SSH1 (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Cortical neurons treated with CXCL12 for one or two hours exhibited a four-fold increase in the F/G-actin ratio relative to vehicle-treated controls.
source: Cortical neurons treated with CXCL12 for one or two hours exhibited a four-fold increase in the F/G-actin ratio relative to vehicle-treated controls, indicative of a shift towards increased actin polymerization (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is supported by F/G-actin ratio assay data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: CXCL12 specifically increased thin spine density on cortical neurons after three hours of treatment.
source: Consistent with our signaling data, CXCL12 specifically increased thin spine density on these neurons (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by spine morphology analysis shown in Figure 6A.

claim: CXCL12 treatment resulted in a reduction in stubby spine density on cortical neurons.
source: On the same segment of dendrite analyzed for thin spine density, we observed a subsequent reduction in stubby spine density.
evidence: This is supported by spine morphology analysis.

claim: Pretreatment with the specific Rac1 inhibitor NSC23766 completely blocked CXCL12-induced activation of Rac1 in cortical neurons.
source: First, we determined that pretreatment of neuronal cultures with the specific Rac1 inhibitor NSC23766 (Gao et al., 2004) (100 µg/mL; 15 mins) completely blocked CXCL12-induced activation of Rac1 (Figure 6B)
evidence: This is supported by Rac1 activity assay data shown in Figure 6B and cited work by Gao et al., 2004.

claim: NSC23766 pretreatment blocked CXCL12-induced phosphorylation of downstream mediators of Rac1.
source: and phosphorylation of its downstream mediators (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Blockade of Rac1 activation by NSC23766 inhibited the ability of CXCL12 to affect overall spine density and thin spine density.
source: As shown in Figure 6D, the ability of CXCL12 to affect overall spine density and thin spine density was inhibited by blockade of Rac1 activation
evidence: This is supported by spine morphology analysis shown in Figure 6D.

claim: NSC23766 did not exhibit any effects on spine density or morphology on its own.
source: furthermore, NSC23766 did not exhibit any effects on spine density or morphology on its own, demonstrating that acute inhibition of Rac1 does not negatively affect dendritic spines.
evidence: This is a negative control finding from the spine morphology analysis.

claim: CXCL12 was unable to modulate spine density or morphology in Rac1 shRNA neurons.
source: Similarly, CXCL12 was unable to modulate spine density or morphology in Rac1 shRNA neurons (Figure 6E)
evidence: This is supported by spine morphology analysis in Rac1 knockdown neurons shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Prolonged inhibition of Rac1 expression by shRNA reduced total spine density.
source: in line with other studies (Tashiro and Yuste, 2004), prolonged inhibition of Rac1 expression by shRNA reduced total spine density (in either vehicle- and CXCL12-treated neurons).
evidence: This is supported by spine density measurements and cited work by Tashiro and Yuste, 2004.

claim: CXCL12 treatment in either WT or HIV-Tg animals resulted in a robust increase in pPAK1 levels compared to vehicle-treated counterparts.
source: While basal level of pPAK in HIV-Tg neurons was lower than WT, CXCL12 treatment in either genotype resulted in a robust increase in pPAK1 levels compared to vehicle-treated counterparts (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemical analysis shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Basal level of pPAK in HIV-Tg neurons was lower than WT.
source: While basal level of pPAK in HIV-Tg neurons was lower than WT, CXCL12 treatment in either genotype resulted in a robust increase in pPAK1 levels compared to vehicle-treated counterparts (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemical analysis shown in Figure 7A.

claim: The effect of CXCL12 on PAK1 activation in HIV-Tg animals resulted in a return to baseline phosphorylation levels.
source: In Tg animals, the effect of CXCL12 on PAK1 activation was as evident as that seen in WT animals, resulting in a return to baseline phosphorylation levels.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the immunohistochemical data.

claim: Levels of pPAK1 in cortical neurons were positively correlated with overall dendritic spine density across all groups.
source: This analysis showed that levels of pPAK1 in cortical neurons were positively correlated with overall dendritic spine density across all groups (Figure 7B)
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Levels of pPAK1 were negatively associated with trials to criterion on the shift to cue phase.
source: while it was negatively associated with trials to criterion on the shift to cue phase (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 7C.

claim: There were no significant changes in total levels of Rac1 protein from frontal cortex lysates of WT and HIV-Tg animals.
source: As predicted by the robust stimulation of pPAK1 in HIV-Tg animals, we observed no significant changes in total levels of Rac1 protein from frontal cortex lysates of WT and Tg animals (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: Untreated HIV-Tg rats have reduced levels of active Rac1 compared to WT animals.
source: Importantly, in line with our observation that Tg animals have lower pPAK1 stimulation at baseline, pulldown studies from PFC tissue of untreated rats demonstrated reduced levels of active Rac1 in Tg rats compared to WT animals (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by Rac1 activity assay data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: Both doses of NSC23766 (1 μg/μL and 2 μg/μL) significantly attenuated activation of Rac1 in frontal cortex lysates in a dose-dependent manner.
source: Immunoblotting revealed that both doses of NSC23766 significantly attenuated activation of Rac1 in frontal cortex lysates in a dose-dependent manner (Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1.

claim: There was a dose-dependent decrease in pPAK1 in NeuN+ cells following NSC23766 treatment.
source: Additionally, there was a dose-dependent decrease in pPAK1 in NeuN+ cells in the contralateral hemisphere (Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemical data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1.

claim: Inhibition of Rac1 was sufficient to prevent the improvement in cognitive flexibility by CXCL12 in WT rats.
source: Inhibition of Rac1 was sufficient to prevent the improvement in cognitive flexibility by CXCL12 as measured by the number of animals reaching criterion (Veh+CXCL12 vs. NSC+CXCL12, p=0.0498) and rate to reach criterion (F(3,32)=12.6622, p<0.001) (Figure 8A and B)
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 8A and 8B.

claim: Cotreatment with NSC23766 blocked upregulation of overall dendritic spine and thin spine density by CXCL12 in WT rats.
source: In the same set of animals used for behavioral analysis, cotreatment with NSC23766 blocked upregulation of overall dendritic spine and thin spine density (Figure 8C and D)
evidence: This is supported by spine morphology analysis shown in Figure 8C and 8D.

claim: NSC23766 prevented decreases in the number of stubby spines induced by CXCL12 in WT rats.
source: and prevented decreases in the number of stubby spines (Figure 8E).
evidence: This is supported by spine morphology analysis shown in Figure 8E.

claim: Overall dendritic spine density in the mPFC across all four groups was inversely correlated to cognitive performance in set-shifting.
source: As previously observed, overall dendritic spine density in the mPFC across all four groups was inversely correlated to cognitive performance in set-shifting (Pearson's r = −0.7862, p=0.0121, α = 0.05; Figure 8F)
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 8F.

claim: The correlation between spine density and set-shifting performance became stronger when only thin spine density was considered in WT rats treated with NSC23766.
source: this correlation became stronger when only thin spine density was considered (Pearson's r = −0.8350, p=0.0058, α = 0.05; Figure 8G).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 8G.

claim: NSC23766 blocked the ability of CXCL12 to recover overall dendritic spine density in HIV-Tg rats.
source: Additionally, NSC23766 blocked the ability of CXCL12 to recover overall dendritic spine density (Figure 9C)
evidence: This is supported by spine morphology analysis shown in Figure 9C.

claim: NSC23766 blocked the ability of CXCL12 to recover thin spine density in HIV-Tg rats.
source: and thin spine density (Figure 9D) in HIV-Tg rats
evidence: This is supported by spine morphology analysis shown in Figure 9D.

claim: NSC23766 blocked the ability of CXCL12 to decrease stubby spine density in HIV-Tg rats.
source: as well as decrease stubby spine density (Figure 9E).
evidence: This is supported by spine morphology analysis shown in Figure 9E.

claim: There was no significant correlation between overall dendritic spine density and TTC in the shift to cue phase in HIV-Tg rats treated with NSC23766.
source: Despite no observed significant correlation between overall dendritic spine density and TTC in the shift to cue phase (Pearson's r = −0.2256, p=0.4808, α=0.05 Figure 9F)
evidence: This is a negative finding from correlation analysis shown in Figure 9F.

claim: There was a strong negative correlation between thin dendritic spine density and shift to cue TTC in HIV-Tg rats treated with NSC23766.
source: there was a strong negative correlation for thin dendritic spine density and shift to cue TTC (Pearson's r = −0.7787, p=0.0029, α = 0.05; Figure 9G).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 9G.

claim: CXCL12 depends on the activation of Rac1 to drive improvements in cognitive flexibility and dendritic spine number in physiological and neuroinflammatory conditions.
source: All together, these data demonstrate that CXCL12 depends on the activation of Rac1 to drive improvements in cognitive flexibility and dendritic spine number in physiological and neuroinflammatory conditions.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the combined data using Rac1 inhibitors in both WT and HIV-Tg rats.

claim: Characterization of executive function deficits in HIV-Tg rats revealed selective alterations in set-shifting, but not initial rule discrimination or reversal learning.
source: Characterization of executive function deficits in HIV-Tg rats revealed selective alterations in set-shifting, but not initial rule discrimination or reversal learning.
evidence: This is a summary of the behavioral findings.

claim: The mPFC, particularly the PrL region, is known to mediate strategy shifting.
source: The mPFC, in particular the PrL region, is known to mediate strategy shifting, as inactivation or lesions to this area specifically impairs this behavioral phenotype while sparing both initial learning and reversal learning (Birrell and Brown, 2000; Floresco et al., 2008).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to Birrell and Brown, 2000 and Floresco et al., 2008.

claim: Damage to the anterior cingulate cortex or orbitofrontal cortex results in deficits in initial rule acquisition or reversal learning respectively.
source: On the other hand, damage to the anterior cingulate cortex or orbitofrontal cortex results in deficits in initial rule acquisition or reversal learning respectively (Hamilton and Brigman, 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation to Hamilton and Brigman, 2015.

claim: Dendritic damage in the context of HIV infection seems to be region specific and very subtle.
source: In line with clinical imaging studies (Sanford et al., 2018; Sanford et al., 2017), dendritic damage in the context of HIV infection seems to be region specific and very subtle.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Sanford et al., 2018 and Sanford et al., 2017.

claim: Stubby spines are considered immature structures due to their usual prevalence during early postnatal development and scarcity in the adult CNS.
source: Stubby spines are considered immature structures due to their usual prevalence during early postnatal development and scarcity in the adult CNS (Harris, 1999).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation to Harris, 1999.

claim: A dendritic spine's head and neck configuration is essential to properly compartmentalize incoming Ca2+ influx through glutamate receptors in order to prevent excitotoxicity.
source: Particularly, a dendritic spine's head and neck configuration is essential to properly compartmentalize incoming Ca2+ influx through glutamate receptors in order to prevent excitotoxicity from occuring (Dong et al., 2009).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation to Dong et al., 2009.

claim: Layer V pyramidal neurons from the PrL region of the mPFC in HIV-Tg rats are hyper-excitable compared to neurons from non-Tg controls.
source: Additionally, electrophysiological data from HIV-Tg rats demonstrated that layer V pyramidal neurons from the PrL region of the mPFC are hyper-excitable compared to neurons from non-Tg controls, as indicated by reduced rheobase, spike amplitude, an inwardly-rectifying K+ influx, increased number of action potentials, and a trend towards aberrant firing (Khodr et al., 2016; Wayman et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Khodr et al., 2016 and Wayman et al., 2016.

claim: This is the first study reporting recovery of both structural and behavioral deficits in the HIV-Tg rat model.
source: Notably, treatment with exogenous CXCL12 completely restored the reduction in dendritic spine density observed in the mPFC of HIV-Tg rats, as well as the associated dysfunction in set-shifting. To our knowledge, this is the first study reporting recovery of both structural and behavioral deficits in the HIV-Tg rat model.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the findings.

claim: Studies were conducted at an age where animals were already impaired, demonstrating that dendritic spine injury and cognitive dysfunction are completely reversible.
source: Importantly, studies were conducted at an age where animals were already impaired, demonstrating that dendritic spine injury and cognitive dysfunction are completely reversible.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental design and findings.

claim: Restoring highly plastic thin spines is a key driver in regulating cognitive function mediated by the mPFC.
source: Our data also suggest that restoring highly plastic thin spines is a key driver in regulating cognitive function mediated by the mPFC.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the correlation data between thin spine density and cognitive performance.

claim: This is the first time the phenomenon of thin spine restoration driving cognitive function has been reported in a rodent model of HAND.
source: This is the first time this phenomenon has been reported in a rodent model of HAND, suggesting that therapeutics to target this spine type are an appropriate strategy to combat the deficits seen in these patients.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the findings.

claim: Extended treatment with CXCL12 did not reveal any side effects in both WT and HIV-Tg animals.
source: Interestingly, the extended treatment with CXCL12 did not reveal any side effects in both WT and Tg animals, indicating that potential effects of the chemokine on other cellular targets (Guyon, 2014) do not interfere with its neuroprotective function - at least within the time frame of this study.
evidence: This is an observation from the behavioral and structural studies, with a citation to Guyon, 2014.

claim: The involvement of the Rac1/PAK pathway in mediating the effects of CXCL12 on actin polymerization has not been described in cortical neurons.
source: The involvement of the Rac1/PAK pathway in mediating the effects of CXCL12 on actin polymerization has not been described in cortical neurons.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the mechanistic findings.

claim: Rac1 activation is the exclusive mediator of CXCL12's alterations on spine density and morphology.
source: Our data show that Rac1 activation is the exclusive mediator of CXCL12's alterations on spine density and morphology, suggesting that targeted therapeutics to selectively activate this pathway through CXCR4 could recover dendritic spine loss.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the Rac1 inhibition and knockdown experiments.

claim: CXCL12 acts on multiple components of the Rac1/PAK pathway to exert control on actin polymerization.
source: This dual regulation of cofilin demonstrates that CXCL12 acts on multiple components of this pathway to exert control on actin polymerization.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the signaling data showing effects on both LIMK1/PAK1 and SSH1.

claim: Blockade of Rac1 activation had no perceived effects on the first two phases of the behavioral task.
source: Interestingly, blockade of Rac1 activation had no perceived effects on the first two phases of the behavioral task, suggesting specificity of the small GTPase in functions mediated by the mPFC but this warrants further investigation.
evidence: This is an observation from the behavioral studies with Rac1 inhibition.

claim: This is the first study to connect Rac1 activation with behavioral flexibility.
source: Nevertheless, to our knowledge, this is the first study to connect Rac1 activation with behavioral flexibility, further underscoring the critical role of the small GTPase in regulating synaptic function.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of connecting Rac1 to cognitive flexibility.

claim: The role of CXCL12/CXCR4 in the developing CNS is well established.
source: The role of CXCL12/CXCR4 in the developing CNS is well established.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field.

claim: The effects of CXCL12 on mature neurons, specifically in the context of synaptic connectivity, are not completely understood.
source: On the other hand, the effects of CXCL12 on mature neurons, specifically in the context of synaptic connectivity, are not completely understood.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: In cortical neurons, induction of Rac1 is associated with F-actin polymerization and spine stability.
source: In cortical neurons, induction of Rac1 is associated with F-actin polymerization and spine stability (Lin and Koleske, 2010).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation to Lin and Koleske, 2010.

claim: Thin spines initially only contain NMDARs and are considered 'silent synapses'.
source: Upregulation of thin spines, which at least initially only contain NMDARs and are considered 'silent synapses', would not be expected to result in significant alterations in synaptic transmission.
evidence: This is established knowledge about thin spine properties.

claim: CXCL12 altered both sEPSC and mEPSC amplitude in whole-cell patch clamp slice recordings.
source: Moreover, our previous work demonstrated that CXCL12 altered both sEPSC and mEPSC amplitude in whole-cell patch clamp slice recordings (Pitcher et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Pitcher et al., 2014.

claim: Changes in mEPSCs amplitude typically reflect alterations to postsynaptic receptors.
source: Changes in mEPSCs amplitude typically reflect alterations to postsynaptic receptors, suggesting that CXCL12 is contributing to the maturation of dendritic spines.
evidence: This is established knowledge in electrophysiology.

claim: Rac1 activation is implicated in spine head morphing, or twitching, that promotes the maturation of synaptic contacts.
source: Furthermore, Rac1 activation is implicated in spine head morphing, or twitching, that promotes the maturation of synaptic contacts (Holtmaat and Svoboda, 2009; Tashiro and Yuste, 2004).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to Holtmaat and Svoboda, 2009 and Tashiro and Yuste, 2004.

claim: Mushroom spines are the most mature and stable spines, typically implicated in long-term memory and potentiation.
source: While we did not observe any changes in mushroom spine density by CXCL12 in vitro or in vivo, this is not surprising given that mushroom spines are the most mature and stable spines, typically implicated in long-term memory and potentiation (Bourne and Harris, 2007).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation to Bourne and Harris, 2007.

claim: CXCL12 can also interact with another receptor, atypical chemokine receptor 3 (ACKR3), also known as CXCR7.
source: It is important to note that the relationship between CXCL12 and CXCR4 is not exclusive, as CXCL12 can also interact with another receptor, atypical chemokine receptor 3 (ACKR3), also known as CXCR7.
evidence: This is established knowledge about CXCL12 receptors.

claim: ACKR3 contains a mutated 'DRYLAIV' motif and thus does not demonstrate G-protein-dependent signaling.
source: ACKR3 contains a mutated 'DRYLAIV' motif (Sierro et al., 2007; Thelen and Thelen, 2008), a region critical for G-protein coupling, and thus does not demonstrate G-protein-dependent signaling.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to Sierro et al., 2007 and Thelen and Thelen, 2008.

claim: ACKR3 is only transiently expressed on the surface of developing neurons and is absent from the cell surface of mature neurons.
source: While the above-mentioned evidence demonstrates that ACKR3 may modulate CXCR4 signaling pathways and responsiveness, the demonstrated absence of cell-surface ACKR3 in mature neurons (ACKR3 is only transiently expressed on the surface of developing neurons) (Shimizu et al., 2011), suggests a predominant role of CXCR4 in CXCL12-mediated effects on dendritic spines and cognition.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Shimizu et al., 2011.

claim: CXCR4 expression has been detected on astrocytes, microglia, and oligodendrocytes.
source: While CXCR4 expression has been detected on other cell types of the CNS, including astrocytes (Bajetto et al., 1999), microglia (Lipfert et al., 2013), and oligodendrocytes (Maysami et al., 2006)
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to Bajetto et al., 1999; Lipfert et al., 2013; and Maysami et al., 2006.

claim: CXCL12's effects on neurons are observed both in the presence and absence of glia.
source: CXCL12's effects on neurons are observed both in the presence and absence of glia (Pitcher et al., 2014; Sengupta et al., 2009)
evidence: This is supported by citations to Pitcher et al., 2014 and Sengupta et al., 2009.

claim: The chemokine's interaction with neuronal CXCR4 is sufficient to induce changes in dendritic spines.
source: and its ability to regulate dendritic spines in cultured neurons is replicated in the intact brain. Thus, the chemokine's interaction with neuronal CXCR4 is sufficient to induce these changes.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the in vitro and in vivo data.

claim: CXCL12 is known to alter GABAergic neurotransmission.
source: CXCL12 is known to alter GABAergic neurotransmission (Bhattacharyya et al., 2008; Guyon and Nahon, 2007)
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to Bhattacharyya et al., 2008 and Guyon and Nahon, 2007.

claim: CXCL12 targets parvalbumin (PV)+ basket interneuron axons and inhibitory perisomatic synapses, which modulates neuronal excitability.
source: Likewise, recent evidence has also shown that CXCL12 targets parvalbumin (PV)+ basket interneuron axons and inhibitory perisomatic synapses, which modulates neuronal excitability (Wu et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Wu et al., 2017.

claim: These studies open the possibility of creating therapeutics to target synaptic and cognitive deficits in HAND patients via restoration of endogenous neuroprotective pathways.
source: In conclusion, these studies open the possibility of creating therapeutics to target synaptic and cognitive deficits in HAND patients via restoration of endogenous neuroprotective pathways.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the study findings.

claim: CXCR4 agonists may be beneficial in alleviating structural and behavioral dysfunction in HAND.
source: While drug discovery involving chemokine receptors has primarily focused on developing antagonists, our work suggests that CXCR4 agonists may be beneficial in alleviating structural and behavioral dysfunction.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the study findings.

claim: Targeting Rac1/PAK signaling pathways may represent a valid strategy for neurorestorative therapies for HAND and other diseases characterized by spine loss and/or CXCR4 dysregulation.
source: Taken together, these data suggest that targeting these signaling pathways may represent a valid strategy for neurorestorative therapies for HAND and other diseases characterized by spine loss and/or CXCR4 dysregulation, such as Alzheimer's disease (AD) and schizophrenia.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the study findings.

claim: Small molecule CXCR4 agonists that may be exploited for further preclinical studies are now available.
source: Interestingly, small molecule CXCR4 agonists that may be exploited for further preclinical studies are now available (Mishra et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Mishra et al., 2016.
